pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** What uses electricity at home

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'identify common appliances that run on electricity.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** National (NGSS): no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation for naming electrical appliances; the nearest energy strand is 4-PS3-2 (energy transferred by electric currents), which this topic only foreshadows. This topic is therefore UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children name and sort everyday appliances by whether they run on electricity and, within that, whether the power comes from the mains (wall socket) or from a battery. No circuit theory, no current, no quantities; the cognitive work is categorisation and safety awareness, not mechanism. The teaching aim is a clean mental sort — mains vs battery vs not-electric — plus the safety habit that mains sockets are dangerous and only batteries are for exploring.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Start from the child's own home: have them name devices in the kitchen, lounge and bedroom, then sort into 'runs on electricity' vs 'does not' (a candle, a wind-up toy, a bicycle are not-electric foils).

Make the mains-vs-battery distinction explicit and physical — show a plug going into a wall socket vs a battery sliding into a torch — because it underpins both the later circuit work (batteries are what you build with) and the safety message (sockets are not).

Embed electrical safety as a non-negotiable: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build. This is a statutory expectation in the surrounding curriculum.
Use sorting and odd-one-out tasks rather than explanation; at this age the learning is reliable categorisation, surfaced and corrected through many quick examples.
Surface edge cases that build flexible thinking: a phone has a battery AND charges from the mains; a car runs on fuel but has electric lights — discuss rather than mark wrong.
keyRepresentations: A labelled scene of a home (kitchen/lounge/bedroom) with tappable appliances — the canonical 'spot the electrical things' picture.
A two-way sort: mains (plug + socket icon) vs battery (cell icon) vs not-electric.
Side-by-side icon pair: a plug entering a wall socket; a battery entering a torch — the mains/battery contrast.
A simple safety symbol/flag attached to mains items ('grown-up only, never poke').
commonMisconceptions: 'Anything that moves or makes noise uses electricity' — children over-include wind-up toys, clockwork and friction-driven things; foils are needed to break this.
'Battery things aren't really electricity' — some children reserve the word for the mains; the battery torch and the wall lamp both use electricity.
'Plugging in charges it up forever' — confusion between charging a battery and being powered while plugged in; not resolved here but worth noting for later.
Treating gas appliances (gas hob, gas fire) as electrical because they are kitchen/heating devices.
Believing the socket itself is 'the electricity' rather than a supply the appliance draws from.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds learning what uses electricity at home (UK KS2 Year 4: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'). The learning goal is a clean three-way mental sort — mains (wall socket) vs battery vs not-electric — anchored in children's own homes, plus the safety habit that mains sockets/plugs/cables are never for experimenting and only battery-powered things are safe to explore. The work is categorisation and safety awareness, not circuit theory, current, or quantities. Deliberate foils (a candle, a wind-up/clockwork toy, a gas hob) break the misconception that anything moving, noisy, or switch-on uses electricity.

activities.title: Spot the electrical things in a home scene
feedback: When a child says a plain wind-up or clockwork TOY uses mains/battery electricity: it moves, but it has no plug and no battery — it stores energy in a wound-up spring and is not electric. (A wind-up RADIO is a different case: it has a small generator and does make its own electricity — see the two-tier check activity.)

When a child calls a gas hob electric because it's in the kitchen and makes heat: trace the energy source — its heat comes from burning gas to make a flame (some hobs use a small electric spark just to light it); contrast with a glowing electric heating element. 'Looks electric, but its heat comes from gas.'

When a child won't call a battery torch electric: both the torch and a wall lamp use electricity — a battery is a portable energy store that supplies electricity when it is connected; mains electricity comes into the home through the socket from power stations and other generators.
On every mains item, reinforce: sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting — grown-up only.
activities.rationale: At this age reliable categorisation is built and corrected through many quick concrete examples starting from the child's own home; a tap-to-reveal home scene delivers the power-source fact and the safety flag on every mains item together, with foils to break over-inclusion.
sourceClaims: Year 4 Electricity statutory requirement: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'; pupils taught to construct simple series circuits and about electrical safety.
Children commonly over-attribute 'uses electricity' to any moving/noisy device and under-attribute it to battery devices; sorting with foils addresses this.
learnerActions: Walk through a labelled home picture (kitchen, lounge, bedroom) and name the devices you see.
Tap or point to each device and say whether it runs on electricity, and if so whether its power comes from the mains (wall socket) or from a battery.

For each device, reveal or state a short fact: e.g. toaster — 'Mains: I plug into the wall. Wall sockets are grown-up only, never poke them'; torch — 'Battery: safe for you to open and explore'; candle or wind-up clock — 'No electricity at all.'
Explain for each item how you can tell — does it have a plug and lead to a socket, or does it carry a battery inside?

Discuss the deliberate foils: a gas hob (may look electric, but its heat comes from burning gas; some use a small electric spark only to light it) and a clockwork/wind-up toy (moves but isn't mains/battery electric).
activities.intendedInsight: The sort isn't simply 'electric or not' but THREE piles — mains, battery, not-electric — and the mains pile is exactly the dangerous one you must never build with, so the only things safe to experiment with are the battery ones.

activities.title: Sort the appliances into three bins
feedback: A wrong drop prompts: 'does it have a plug or a battery?' before retrying.
Edge-case cards (phone, car) open a short 'both!' / 'neither, really' explainer rather than being marked right or wrong.
If a child sorts only by 'has a plug', point out the battery torch is still electric, and a gas hob gets its heat from burning gas even though some are plugged in for a spark igniter.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-sort bench makes categorisation active and self-correcting and doubles as quick formative assessment; immediate right/wrong feedback helps build the sort, not just test it.
sourceClaims: Children commonly over-attribute 'uses electricity' to any moving/noisy device and under-attribute it to battery devices; sorting with foils addresses this.
learnerActions: Take a set of appliance cards and place each into one of three labelled bins: Mains, Battery, Not electric.
For a wrong placement, use the hint 'does it have a plug or a battery?' and try again.

Handle edge-case cards (a phone, a car) by discussing rather than scoring: a phone has a battery AND charges from the mains; a petrol or diesel car burns fuel to move but uses a battery for its electric lights, while an electric car runs on a big battery.
Name at least ten appliances and place them, then say aloud the rule you used to sort.
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting by energy source (mains vs battery vs not-electric) is an active, self-correcting way to build and firm up the mental model, and edge cases show the piles aren't always clean-cut.

activities.title: Odd-one-out and power-source matching
feedback: If the odd-one-out is chosen by looks alone, ask which energy source each one uses.
For a wrong match, restate: mains items have a plug/lead to a wall socket; battery items carry their energy inside with no plug.
activities.rationale: Odd-one-out and matching cleanly check the sort. Note that recognition tasks like these assess and firm up the model more than they build it, so use them alongside the exploratory scene and the sorting bench.
learnerActions: Given a small group of appliances, pick the odd one out (e.g. the one that does not run on electricity) and say why.
Match each device to its power source (mains socket icon vs battery/cell icon).
Answer 'which of these run on electricity?' and justify the choice by energy source, not just by appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick recognition tasks let a learner check and firm up the mains/battery/not-electric sort across many examples.

activities.title: Ask the electrician: why and what's safe
feedback: The character always returns to the rule: wall sockets are grown-up only, never poke them.

For 'is the gas cooker electric?' the answer traces the energy source: it cooks with heat from burning gas, not electricity (some have a small electric spark or light, but that is not what cooks the food).
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue can reinforce the safety habit and answer 'why?' questions. The core target skill is silent sorting, so treat this as a supplement rather than the main vehicle.
sourceClaims: Year 4 Electricity statutory requirement: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'; pupils taught to construct simple series circuits and about electrical safety.
learnerActions: Pose questions to an in-role 'electrician' character, e.g. 'is the toaster electric?' or 'why can't I poke the socket?'
Ask 'where does the electricity come from?' for a mains item and for a battery item, and compare the answers.
Restate the safety rule in your own words: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through 'why' reinforces the safety habit and the idea that mains and battery are both electricity from different supplies.

activities.title: Two-tier check: four things, which use electricity and how?
feedback: Full answer: the battery torch and mains fridge use electricity; the gas cooker gets its cooking heat from burning gas (some have a small electric spark to light it); the wind-up radio makes its own electricity because winding it turns a small generator, so it can work with no plug (some models store that electricity in a built-in rechargeable battery). Mains items have a plug/lead to a socket; battery ones carry energy inside with no plug.

Gap pattern ('no plug, no electricity'): sort by energy source, not plug — a battery is a portable energy store that supplies electricity, and the wind-up radio generates its own with a small generator.
If the gas cooker is labelled electric: its cooking heat comes from burning gas to make a flame (any electric spark only lights it); contrast with a glowing electric heating element.

If the torch is denied as electric: both mains and a battery supply electricity to make things work; mains electricity comes through the socket from power stations and other generators, while a battery is a portable energy store that supplies electricity when it is connected.
activities.rationale: A two-tier diagnostic with a reason tier discriminates children who equate 'has a plug' with 'uses electricity' (they miss the wind-up radio and may include the gas cooker) from those who reason about the energy source.
learnerActions: Look at four things: a torch that takes batteries, a gas cooker, a wind-up radio, and a fridge plugged into the wall.
Say which ones use electricity to work.
For the ones that do, say how you can tell which get their electricity from the mains and which from a battery.

Answer deeper probes: how can a wind-up radio with no battery and no plug still use electricity? When a phone is plugged in, is it mains or battery, and what's happening to the battery? Name three things at home that make heat — which get that heat from electricity and which from burning something? If the power cut off in your street, which of the four things would still work, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying by electrical energy source (mains vs battery vs self-generated) — rather than by 'has a plug' — is what separates a surface sort from real understanding, and extends to new cases like a power cut or a phone charging.

constraints: No circuit theory, current, or quantities at this stage; the cognitive work is categorisation and safety awareness, not mechanism.
Electrical safety is non-negotiable and a statutory expectation: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build.

Recognition tasks (odd-one-out, matching) assess and firm up the model more than they build it, so pair them with other activities; the interactive drag-to-sort bench, by contrast, is active and self-correcting and does help build the sort as well as check it.
The in-role electrician dialogue is a useful supplement for 'why' and safety, not the main vehicle, since the target skill is silent sorting.
Edge cases (phone that is both battery and mains-charging; car that runs on fuel but has electric lights) should be discussed rather than marked right/wrong.
'Plugging in charges a battery forever' / the confusion between charging and being powered while plugged in is not resolved at this level but is worth flagging for later.

A flat labelled scene teaches the categorisation adequately; a 3D navigable house adds navigation cost without teaching the sort better, so a spatial/3D treatment is not needed here (this is not a claim that 3D cannot teach).
Distinguish a plain wind-up/clockwork toy (mechanical, not electric) from a wind-up radio (has a small generator and does produce electricity); do not let one blanket rule cover both.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOP Spark / SPT children's ideas about electricity) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its misconception claim as indicative, not confirmed.

The learner-level phrasings 'a battery is a portable store of electrical energy' and the wind-up radio 'makes its own electricity' are age-appropriate simplifications (a battery stores chemical energy converted to electrical current; a wind-up device stores elastic/mechanical energy driving a small generator). Kept as the original row stated them, but flagged so reviewers can decide how precise to be for this age.
The US NGSS mapping notes no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation for naming electrical appliances (nearest is 4-PS3-2, only foreshadowed); this topic is UK-anchored.
Product/artefact-type names, fit rankings, and quiz-step vocabulary from the source were removed; the underlying tasks and feedback were preserved.

The DfE statutory claim is mapped to activities that concretely deliver its safety message; it is a curriculum/convention source, not evidence that any proposed activity is effective or superior to another medium.

probeDeeper: The wind-up radio has no battery and no plug. How can it still be using electricity?
A phone can run while plugged in AND unplugged. Is it mains or battery — and what's happening to the battery when it's plugged in?
Name three things at home that make heat: which get that heat from electricity and which from burning something?
If the power cut off in your street, which of your four things would still work, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The battery torch and the mains fridge use electricity; the gas cooker burns gas, not electricity; the wind-up radio makes its own electricity from a spring you wind, so it uses electricity but needs no battery or plug. Mains appliances have a plug/lead to a wall socket; battery ones carry their energy inside a battery and have no plug.

errorPatterns.pattern: Anything with a plug or that you switch on uses electricity, and anything without a plug doesn't ('no plug, no electricity').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort by ENERGY SOURCE, not by plug — mains, battery, wind-up/other; show that a battery is a portable store of electrical energy.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only the fridge uses electricity, because it's the only one plugged into the wall.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the wind-up radio isn't electrical and can't classify battery devices.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gas and electric appliances are the same because both switch on and both make heat ('it's all electric really').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the energy source — gas burns a fuel to make a flame; contrast that with a glowing electric heating element.
errorPatterns.distractor: The gas cooker uses electricity, because you turn it on to make heat like the others.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the gas cooker as electric.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mains and battery electricity are two completely different things, not both electricity ('battery isn't real electricity').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Both deliver an electric current to make the device work; mains comes from a power station through the socket, a battery is a portable store of the same thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Won't call the torch electric, or treats battery power as a separate kind of thing.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by 'has a plug' alone; calls the gas cooker electric or the wind-up/battery device non-electric.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by electrical energy source — mains vs battery vs self-generated — explains that gas burns fuel rather than using electricity, and applies it to a new case such as a power cut or a phone charging.
responseLevels.partial: Names many electrical appliances and knows some run on batteries, but can't consistently sort by energy SOURCE (misses the wind-up radio, or lumps the gas cooker in).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at these four things: a torch that takes batteries, a gas cooker, a wind-up radio, and a fridge plugged into the wall. Which ones use electricity to work, and how can you tell which get their electricity from the mains and which from a battery?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who equates 'has a plug' with 'uses electricity' misses the wind-up radio and may wrongly include the gas cooker; the reason tier separates 'plugged in = electric' from 'the energy source is an electric current'.
